# Fog-of-War Chess: Complete Experiment and Findings History

Consolidated on **2026-11-04 (America/New_York)**. Repository: `/Users/jesuscaraball0/code/school_code/67980/fow`.

**This is the single source of truth for supervised/imitation experiment findings. RL findings, including PPO and critic-fitting experiments, are maintained in [RL_EXPERIMENT_HISTORY.md](RL_EXPERIMENT_HISTORY.md).** Raw metrics/checkpoints/replays are the underlying evidence; other project documentation covers operation and setup, not a parallel findings record. This document combines the locally retained numerical artifacts, historical Markdown analyses, and findings discussed in the working conversation. It covers successful runs, partial/failed attempts, reused references, negative results, instrumentation changes, and unresolved hypotheses. It does **not** invent results for missing artifacts or the newly submitted medium residual run.

## How to read this record

The numbered stages below follow experiment history. Timestamped training folders ending in `Z` use UTC; November UTC timestamps are five hours ahead of local Eastern time. Older evaluation folder timestamps have no timezone marker and are reported verbatim. Cluster job IDs and the conversation establish the placement of downloaded runs where the local copy time is not the original training time. Parallel launches can overlap; their listing order does not assert completion order.

**Evidence priority:** saved primary metrics/checkpoints and evaluation summaries take priority over conversational impressions; saved reports supply additional post-hoc analyses; conversation-only observations are explicitly labeled. Historical recommendations are retained as historical, and revised conclusions are stated where later evidence contradicts them. Missing metrics are not reconstructed as measured results.

**Coverage:** all locally discovered training `metrics.json` records and saved evaluation summaries are catalogued below. Reused references are not counted as independent evidence. The original raw artifacts remain the source of full per-step LR traces, per-channel arrays, histogram bins, split manifests, RNG states, and game replays; this document records all run outcomes and aggregate diagnostic findings rather than reproducing millions of raw values. No independent test set has been established by this work; repeated validation-driven experimentation can adapt to the held-out games.

The 20 all-draw games repeated lengths 49/52 plies and ended by threefold repetition. This is consistent with deterministic argmax trajectories cycling from the same initial board; it does not establish equal playing strength. Later sampling produced varied games. The 66–34 and 63–37 series are the exact user-reported results preserved in saved summaries; the recurrent checkpoint hash differs in the latter series. “King capturable” is the fog-of-war referee’s terminal condition, not a bot-process failure or necessarily an illegal move.

<a id="stage-2"></a>

## 2. Bot split, sampling, visible king safety, and recurrent interpretation

The implementation was split into `starters/neural`, `starters/neural_recurrent`, and reusable `starters/shared` code so future policies (including possible PPO policies) can play each other through the same protocol. The evaluator snapshots bots/checkpoints before a series and records hashes, colors, failures, move counts, and termination reasons.

Inference changed from argmax to sampling only over available move candidates at temperature **0.9**. A lower temperature sharpens the distribution; this choice was requested, not optimized by a temperature sweep. Stochastic sampling breaks deterministic cycling but does not guarantee a stronger policy.

The observation move tracker gained **visible king-safety filtering**: avoid moves that leave the king capturable based on the information available in the observation. This is not access to a hidden global board and cannot guarantee safety against an unseen attacker. Legal action candidates, visible-safety filtering, and game terminal rules are distinct. Therefore “King capturable: 100” alone does not demonstrate that the filter is broken.

The recurrent policy uses a CNN encoder followed by a GRUCell; recurrence adds memory, not a promise of stronger play. Memory state belongs to a player’s game history and is reset between independent games/batches. It is detached at truncated-BPTT boundaries. More parameters, correlated replay positions, learning dynamics, and the supervision target all affect whether it learns useful history. No evidence here establishes that recurrence must outperform feedforward imitation learning.

<a id="stage-3"></a>

## 3. First full-data diagnostic retraining: feedforward and recurrent (November 2 local / November 3 UTC)

Both diagnostic retraining runs used the complete fixed 90/10 split: **55,250 training games / 5,350,942 labeled positions**, **6,141 validation games / 595,179 positions**, seed 7980, 50 epochs, Adam LR 1e-3. The feedforward run used MPS locally; the recurrent run used CUDA on the cluster. Their batching/update counts differ, so 50 epochs is not equal optimizer exposure.

Feedforward: best validation NLL **2.474178 at epoch 40**, final **2.483019**, final raw accuracy **31.428%**, best recorded raw accuracy **31.612% at epoch 45**. Recurrent: best validation NLL **2.690992 at epoch 26**, final **2.714629**, final raw accuracy **29.866%**, best recorded raw accuracy **30.248% at epoch 34**. These show some late validation-loss deterioration, especially relative to their best epochs, but do not justify describing all later runs as severely overfit.

The recurrent final-epoch convolutional gradient maxima reach tens of millions before clipping (encoder.0 max **27,809,872**), with mean norms dominated by rare large events. Its global clipping threshold was historically 1; the feedforward clipping hook was a no-op. Thus we did not originally have the later common clip-5 recipe on both architectures.

The duplicated recurrent job checkpoints/folders were discussed and one redundant run directory was removed. The retained directory records job 27721607 in its config; both `recurrent-job-27721603.pt` and `recurrent-job-27721607.pt` still exist as loose files. Their existence is not evidence of two independent seeds or two independent completed diagnostic runs. Historical claims that they were the same run should not be elevated to a new independent result.

<a id="stage-4"></a>

## 4. Diagnostic expansion and metric interpretation

Training diagnostics were added after the early king-capturability and recurrence questions: per-epoch train/validation loss, learning rates, per-layer gradient L2 before/after clipping, saved JSON, and final weight/activation histograms. Subsequent diagnostics added raw/legal NLL and accuracy, legal probability mass and entropy, safety-removal measures, gradient medians/p95/max and clipping fractions, actual sampled optimizer update-to-weight ratios, per-channel activation summaries, recurrent reset-memory ablations, and gradient-by-history-lag probes.

The user initially saw almost-zero ReLU histograms and mostly negative preactivations. These were valid concerns, but early histograms were sampled distributions. A large near-zero histogram bin is not an exact count of zero activations, and sparse ReLU activity alone does not prove permanently dead features. Later exact sampled-observation statistics distinguish zero rate, relative dormancy, and channel concentration.

The encoder indices describe modules, not separate networks: encoder.0 and encoder.2 were convolutions; .1 and .3 their ReLUs; .4 flatten; .5 a dense projection; .6 its ReLU. `policy` maps features to 4,096 move classes; `value` is an auxiliary head not supervised by the imitation loss, so its missing gradients/random output are expected. `memory` is the recurrent GRU. The flattened dense projection means these models are CNN-plus-dense policies, not convolution-only models. Layer names changed internally for BN and residual blocks; named module lookup is required rather than assuming Sequential position equals the historical numeric key.

The metric review removed unwanted channel/sparsity/memory-saturation plot outputs rather than adding switches for every plot. Exact activation statistics continued to support later analysis; the retained runs still include dormant-feature plots. Healthy activations need not be Gaussian, and ReLU activations cannot have a symmetric normal distribution. Signed preactivations, post-ReLU activity, BN parameters, and policy logits have different expected roles.

The apparent improvement in later small-model activations coincided with changes in model capacity, data exposure, and training settings. It was not a controlled demonstration that changing ReLU to LeakyReLU alone fixed the original problem. Diagnostic sampling uses an independent reservoir RNG; later matched experiments additionally control training RNG consumed by evaluation.

<a id="stage-6"></a>

## 6. Completed small-data activation and recurrence matrix

The rerun completed all eight combinations: feedforward/recurrent × ReLU/LeakyReLU × 32/128 training games, now eight epochs, one seed 7980. Architecture dimensions were 8/32; validation used 16 games / 1,470 moves; policy probes used only 128 positions and activation probes 64 observations. These were pipeline/learning sanity experiments, not realistic final accuracy estimates.

With 32 games, LeakyReLU slightly reduced feedforward final raw NLL (6.8360 → 6.7930), but slightly reduced raw accuracy; with 128 games, ReLU had slightly better raw NLL (5.9660 versus 5.9776). The recurrent 32-game models worsened from their best validation NLLs and resetting memory modestly improved probe NLL (negative reset-minus-normal deltas). With 128 games, retaining history improved probe NLL (positive deltas ~0.082 and ~0.116). This is evidence that the reset-memory probe can detect history utility, not proof of robust recurrent superiority. The exact per-case curves, lag profiles, and diagnostics follow.

<a id="stage-7"></a>

## 7. Fixed-update size comparison with Adam

To separate model-size effects from uneven epoch/update exposure, the next sweep used the same 512 training games (**49,727 moves**), 64 validation games (**6,147 moves**), identical input batch streams, one seed, batch 128, and saved checkpoints at 200 / 1,000 / 2,000 updates. Small 8/32 had 153,217 parameters; original 64/256 had 2,146,817. Optimizer was Adam at LR 1e-3.

The original model learned faster and reached a much better best validation NLL (**4.6477 at 1,000 updates**) than the small model (**5.5707 at 2,000**). The large model’s later raw NLL worsened while accuracy continued improving. This distinguishes a budget-dependent capacity benefit from a claim that the largest model is always best or always too large.

## 8. Same comparison with AdamW

The same size sweep was repeated with AdamW, LR 1e-3 and weight decay 0.01. Both best validation losses decreased slightly: small **5.5707 → 5.5669**, original **4.6477 → 4.6453**. Calling the losses unchanged would be inaccurate; calling these tiny one-seed differences a major gain would also overstate the evidence. Exact final accuracy and per-checkpoint diagnostics are below.

<a id="stage-9"></a>

## 9. Lower-LR AdamW comparison

The user specified AdamW LR **1e-4**, beta1 **0.9**, beta2 **0.99**, weight decay **0.01**, epsilon **1e-8**. With the same 2,000-update budget, the small model reached NLL **6.2870**, original **5.5077**: both worse than their higher-LR counterparts at that budget. This supports slower learning under the lower LR, not a universal conclusion that a lower LR cannot help longer-run stability. Changing both LR and beta2 means it was not an isolated LR-only intervention.

Suite source: `/Users/jesuscaraball0/code/school_code/67980/fow/out/experiments/size-adamw-lr1e-4-beta099-512games-2000updates/experiment.json`; recorded suite status: **completed**.

<a id="stage-10"></a>

## 10. Small-model warmup and cosine decay

The small model alone was trained for the complete requested eight epochs, without a short precheck: three epochs of linear warmup from 1e-4 to 1e-3, followed by five epochs of cosine decay to **1e-5** (the chat’s “1e5” was interpreted as 1e-5). With 512 games this means 3,104 updates, not 2,000; best/final raw NLL was **5.6192**, final accuracy **7.044%**. The suite settings retain an old nominal checkpoint list, but the actual metrics record eight epoch-aligned checkpoints. Always use recorded updates rather than stale requested defaults.

Suite source: `/Users/jesuscaraball0/code/school_code/67980/fow/out/experiments/small-cnn-warmup-cosine-512games-8epochs/experiment.json`; recorded suite status: **completed**.

## 11. Five-times-more-games small-model run

Training games increased fivefold, 512 → **2,560**, and moves increased from 49,727 to **248,396**, keeping eight epochs and the three-plus-five-epoch schedule. This expanded the update budget to **15,520** and warmup to **5,820** updates. The small model’s best/final raw NLL improved to **4.5191**, accuracy **13.747%**. This changes both distinct data and optimizer updates; it is not a fixed-compute causal estimate of data scaling.

<a id="stage-12"></a>

## 12. Medium plain CNN on the same setup

The medium plain CNN (32 channels / 128 hidden; **804,097 parameters**, no BN) ran on the same 2,560/64-game setup and 15,520-update schedule. Best raw NLL was **3.4588 at 13,580 updates**; final accuracy **21.376%**. It was the most attractive practical compromise in that size sweep: far stronger than the small model and less late raw-NLL degradation than the full model. The user noted balanced-looking distributions and gradients; these are supporting diagnostics, not the optimization objective or proof of an optimal capacity.

Suite source: `/Users/jesuscaraball0/code/school_code/67980/fow/out/experiments/medium-cnn-warmup-cosine-2560games-8epochs/experiment.json`; recorded suite status: **completed**.

## 13. Full plain CNN on the same setup

The full plain CNN (64/256; **2,146,817 parameters**, no BN) ran in parallel under the same data and update schedule. Best raw NLL was **3.4073 at 9,700 updates**, better than medium’s best, while final raw NLL deteriorated substantially (about 3.703) and final accuracy reached **22.743%**. Thus “medium healthiest” and “full highest accuracy” could both be true; final loss, best loss, accuracy, and internal statistics ranked models differently. The small-data late overfitting did not establish that 2.15m parameters would be excessive on the full dataset.

<a id="stage-14"></a>

## 14. He-normal convolution initialization

A medium CNN rerun changed only convolution weights to He-normal initialization; dense/output initialization remained as specified by the runner. Best raw NLL was **3.5066**, worse than default initialization’s **3.4588**; final raw accuracy was **21.230%** versus default **21.376%**. Final raw NLL was also worse (about 3.552 versus 3.469). He normal is theoretically motivated for ReLU variance propagation, but it did not improve this controlled seed. This is evidence to retain the default recipe here, not a general refutation of He initialization.

Suite source: `/Users/jesuscaraball0/code/school_code/67980/fow/out/experiments/medium-cnn-he-normal-2560games-8epochs/experiment.json`; recorded suite status: **completed**.

<a id="stage-15"></a>

## 15. Larger-data peak-LR and convolutional BatchNorm experiments

The next three runs used the full 64/256 CNN, **12,800 training games / 1,238,282 positions**, the same 64 validation games / 6,147 moves, and the same **15,520 updates**. Warmup stayed at 5,820 updates and decay at 9,700, so data exposure was fewer passes than in the 2,560-game experiment. Runs compared peak LR 1e-3, peak LR 3e-4, and convolutional BN with peak 1e-3. All used AdamW (0.9,0.99), eps 1e-8, decay .01.

Final raw NLL / accuracy: higher peak **2.9593 / 25.931%**, lower peak **3.1808 / 22.336%**, BN higher peak **2.8752 / 26.924%**. Convolutional BN helped this short run; reducing the peak LR did not improve predictions at this budget. BN adds 256 trainable parameters to this architecture (2,147,073 total).

The 128-position legal probe initially suggested misleading relative rankings. Re-evaluation on all 6,147 held-out positions showed BN best: legal NLL **2.7464**, legal accuracy **27.217%**, versus no-BN higher-peak **2.7899 / 26.338%**, lower-peak **2.9369 / 22.905%**. This is direct evidence for reporting probe size and checking small-probe conclusions. These short runs did not establish long-run BN stability.

Suite source: `/Users/jesuscaraball0/code/school_code/67980/fow/out/experiments/full-cnn-12800games-peak-lr1e-3/experiment.json`; recorded suite status: **completed**.

<a id="stage-16"></a>

## 16. First full-data cluster CNN with AdamW, BN, and clip 5

Cluster job **27800942** trained the full 64/256 CNN with convolutional BN, AdamW (0.9,0.99), eps 1e-8, decay .01, batch 128, global clip **5**, default initialization, ReLU, and no dropout. It used all 55,250 training games / 5,350,942 moves and all 6,141 validation games / 595,179 moves.

Although a larger run had been discussed, the actual completed run was **8 epochs / 334,440 updates**, not 50. It completed its entire LR schedule, warmup 5,820 from 1e-4 to 1e-3, cosine to 1e-5. Best validation NLL was the final epoch (**2.580976**), raw accuracy **30.98%**. Training NLL fell to **2.4891**. Validation continued improving: this is not the small-data overfitting pattern.

The user’s concern about internal health was well founded: global pre-clip median rose roughly 2.61 → 20.46; clipping rose 4.41% → 53.98% → 99.63%, then 100% from epoch 4. Largest global norm ~104.8; second BN affine gradient max ~103.7. Final BN2 gamma median ~0.0527 and beta median ~-0.108; running variances remained finite/reasonable (~0.164–0.852).

Additional checkpoint analysis discussed in chat found dense weight L2 ~505 (from ~117 at epoch 1), policy L2 ~2,648 (from ~655). Last conv ReLU ~96.3% zeros, 11/64 relatively dormant channels; dense ~27.3% dormant. Five conv channels carried ~89.2% of activity; four dense units ~91.3%. These are sampled activity measures, not causal contribution.

Fresh 128-observation gradient probes were finite: train-mode global ~27.25 with BN2 affine ~81.4% of squared gradient norm; eval ~17.47 with ~49%. Losses ~2.736 vs ~2.716 did not suggest completely broken BN buffers. Covariance analysis on a fresh random 512 observations across 64 games found low raw-scale effective ranks (trunk ~2.17; dense ~1.68) but much larger standardized ranks (~30.75 / ~140.51), indicating scale imbalance rather than proof that all but a few features contain zero information. The full numerical covariance/probe script outputs are not retained as a standalone artifact; these approximate values are conversation-recorded analyses, distinct from the primary per-epoch metrics below.

Operational findings: ORCD job scripts use `mit_normal_gpu`, one GPU, four CPU cores, 32 GiB RAM and six-hour limits. The missing-torch failure came from an incorrect/incomplete Python environment; `.venv-cnn` later confirmed Torch 2.11.0+cu128. SSH/Duo/network timeouts are not evidence of a training failure. Slurm jobs continue after SSH disconnects. Large rsync scans of the replay tree can appear stalled; code-only sync excludes data/results. The configured production trainer supports epoch-boundary resume with optimizer, scheduler, model/BN buffers, CPU/CUDA RNG and loader-generator state.

<a id="stage-17"></a>

## 17. Normalization and weight-decay stability ablations

Four matched stability experiments used a smaller BN CNN (16 channels / 64 hidden), **2,560 training games / 248,396 moves**, 64 validation games / 6,147 moves, seed 7980, batch 128, AdamW (0.9,0.99), eps 1e-8, decay .01, clip5, **80,000 updates**. They intentionally used only the first 80k updates of the earlier 334,440-update LR schedule. Actual LR at 80k was still ~8.81e-4; the run had repeated its small dataset ~41 times. This was a matched stress-test design, not a scheduler bug.

Controls: baseline; exclude norm/bias from decay; fixed BN affine (no learned gamma/beta); dense BN. No-decay was nearly neutral. Fixed affine worsened NLL and clipping. Dense BN balanced dense activity but did not consistently improve final predictions. Crucially the smaller baseline had **zero late clipping**, so this suite did not reproduce the full CNN’s sustained clipping. Do not call a remedy validated on this suite a proven fix for the full model.

Suite source: `/Users/jesuscaraball0/code/school_code/67980/fow/out/experiments/normalization-weight-decay-ablations-2560games-80k/experiment.json`; recorded suite status: **completed**.

### Preserved analysis from this stage

Retired report, merged into this document: `/Users/jesuscaraball0/code/school_code/67980/fow/out/experiments/normalization-weight-decay-ablations-2560games-80k/report.md`. This preserves the stage-specific assessment. Later sections supersede provisional recommendations where evidence changed.

### Stability ablation results

Four matched runs: 16 channels / 64 features, 2,560 training games, 64 validation games (6,147 moves), seed 7980, batch 128, AdamW (0.9, 0.99), epsilon 1e-8, weight decay 0.01, and global clipping at 5.

Each ran 80,000 updates from the beginning of the cluster run's 334,440-update LR schedule. Inputs and order match across all cases. The smaller training dataset is repeated about 41 times.

| Case | Best observed val loss | Best update | Final val loss | Final accuracy | Final legal NLL | Late clipping | Top-four dense activity |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Baseline | 3.7138 | 40,000 | 3.7915 | 20.7% | 3.5297 | 0.0% | 47.6% |
| No decay on norms/bias | 3.7140 | 40,000 | 3.7809 | 20.6% | 3.5089 | 0.0% | 47.6% |
| Fixed BN affine | 3.8039 | 20,000 | 4.0995 | 18.9% | 3.7737 | 42.8% | 49.3% |
| Dense BatchNorm | 3.6913 | 20,000 | 3.8004 | 20.3% | 3.5143 | 0.0% | 11.9% |

Late clipping covers updates 40,001–80,000. Activation metrics use a fixed random sample of 512 held-out moves; final legal metrics cover all 6,147 validation moves.

Dense normalization reduces activity concentration from 47.6% to 11.9% and late median gradient norm from 3.41 to 2.82. Its best validation loss improves slightly, but final validation loss and accuracy do not improve. Excluding normalization/bias from decay is almost neutral. Fixing BN affine parameters worsens validation and increases late clipping.

Limitation: the smaller baseline does not reproduce the full run's near-universal clipping. These results support dense normalization as a feature-balance intervention but do not establish a fix for the full-model instability. One seed, substantial small-data overfitting, and best values selected from saved checkpoints.

Next: retain learned BN affine parameters. Confirm dense normalization against the full architecture and intended LR horizon through 80k–120k updates, tracking clipping, per-layer gradient shares, BN gamma/beta, and feature concentration. The weight-decay change is not a proven fix.

Reproduce: `.venv/bin/python training/stability_experiment.py`

## 18. Dropout and dense-BN-plus-dropout ablations

Four cases repeated the same cached data, dimensions, 80k exposure, seed and LR stream: no dropout, hidden dropout .1, hidden dropout .2, dense BN plus hidden dropout .1. Dropout follows the dense ReLU and is disabled in evaluation. It was not part of the earlier full-data cluster CNN; earlier assumptions that we already had it were corrected.

Dropout .1 gave the strongest balanced NLL/accuracy result of these cases: final raw NLL **3.6342** versus baseline **3.7915**, dense top-four activity **12.85%** versus **47.65%**. Dropout .2 reduced concentration further but had lower accuracy and more late clipping. Dense BN plus dropout achieved the lowest dense concentration (~9.44%) and stable gradients, but did not beat dropout .1 on final prediction metrics. Thus better-looking feature balance is not automatically better prediction quality.

The baseline exactly reproduced the prior baseline’s checkpoints/final weights, demonstrating reproducibility rather than independent-seed confirmation. Batch hashes and LR traces matched all cases. Parameter norms increased in some dropout cases despite more balanced activations; subtracting the common action-logit offset reduced norms without changing softmax. Weight norms by themselves are not a quality metric.

Suite source: `/Users/jesuscaraball0/code/school_code/67980/fow/out/experiments/dropout-dense-bn-ablations-2560games-80k/experiment.json`; recorded suite status: **completed**.

### Preserved analysis from this stage

Retired report, merged into this document: `/Users/jesuscaraball0/code/school_code/67980/fow/out/experiments/dropout-dense-bn-ablations-2560games-80k/report.md`. This preserves the stage-specific assessment. Later sections supersede provisional recommendations where evidence changed.

### Matched dropout comparison

One seed (7980); 16 convolutional channels / 64 hidden features; identical cached 2,560 training games (248,396 moves) and 64 validation games (6,147 moves). Batch 128; 80,000 updates; AdamW betas (0.9, 0.99), epsilon 1e-8, weight decay 0.01; global gradient clipping at 5. All variants retain convolutional BatchNorm and default initialization. Learning rate uses the first 80,000 updates of the 334,440-update cluster schedule: warmup 5,820 updates from 1e-4 to 1e-3, then cosine decay toward 1e-5. Dropout follows the dense ReLU and is off during evaluation.

#### Prediction results

| Variant | Best saved val loss | Update | Final val loss | Final raw top-1 | Final legal NLL | Final legal top-1 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| baseline | 3.7138 | 40,000 | 3.7915 | 20.69% | 3.5297 | 21.46% |
| dropout_01 | 3.6342 | 80,000 | 3.6342 | 20.74% | 3.2746 | 21.57% |
| dropout_02 | 3.6515 | 80,000 | 3.6515 | 20.12% | 3.2410 | 20.92% |
| dense_bn_dropout_01 | 3.6436 | 40,000 | 3.6690 | 20.42% | 3.3154 | 21.31% |

Best means best among the four saved checkpoints; final legal metrics cover all 6,147 held-out moves.

#### Comparison with previous dense BatchNorm run

Dense BatchNorm alone: best saved val loss 3.6913 at 20,000 updates; final val loss 3.8004; final raw top-1 20.27%; top four dense activity share 11.85%.

#### Validation and limits

The baseline exactly reproduces the previous round at every checkpoint, including final model weights. All four actual input batch hashes and per-update LR traces match. Gradients remain finite; clipping respects the threshold within float32 norm-reduction tolerance. All 37 repository tests passed.

This is a one-seed comparison on a heavily reused dataset (about 41 passes). It does not establish playing strength or solve the large model instability: the medium baseline does not reproduce sustained 100% clipping. Training losses include active dropout for the dropout variants and should not be compared as if evaluated under identical deterministic conditions.

#### Final parameter norms

| Variant | Dense weight L2 | Policy weight L2 | Policy L2 after removing common logit offset |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| baseline | 52.93 | 573.44 | 388.95 |
| dropout_01 | 52.53 | 1182.41 | 655.84 |
| dropout_02 | 64.09 | 1584.32 | 947.53 |
| dense_bn_dropout_01 | 52.96 | 1158.14 | 589.15 |

Subtracting the action-wise mean weight vector removes a shared contribution to all logits, which leaves softmax probabilities unchanged. Norms alone do not measure prediction quality.

<a id="stage-19"></a>

## 19. Residual depth and reduced-head architecture ablations

Two new architectures were trained against a **copied** dropout-.1 reference. Equal data, updates, seed, dimensions and LR trace were maintained; compute was not equal because depth changed. Residual: one stem plus three two-convolution post-activation identity-shortcut blocks (seven spatial convolutions, theoretical receptive field 15×15 versus 5×5). Reduced head: original two-conv trunk plus a 1×1 projection from 16 to 4 channels before flattening; dense width remains 64.

The residual model had **348,081 parameters**, only ~3.5% above the 336,321-parameter BN reference. It improved raw and legal accuracy: final raw **22.22%** versus **20.74%**, legal **23.07%** versus **21.57%**. Best saved raw NLL **3.5724 at 40k** beat the reference, but its final legal NLL was worse and late clipping reached **12.84%**. Trunk activity concentrated more, not less. This tests depth and shortcuts together, not the isolated benefit of identity shortcuts.

Reduced head used **287,237 parameters**, ~14.6% fewer than reference. It improved raw/legal NLL but reduced raw/legal top-1 accuracy. It is a parameter-efficiency/probability-quality tradeoff, not an accuracy win. Common stem/dense/output initialization and training RNG were preserved where shapes allowed; extra layers initialized under a forked RNG.

Suite source: `/Users/jesuscaraball0/code/school_code/67980/fow/out/experiments/residual-reduced-head-ablations-2560games-80k/experiment.json`; recorded suite status: **completed**.

### Preserved analysis from this stage

Retired report, merged into this document: `/Users/jesuscaraball0/code/school_code/67980/fow/out/experiments/residual-reduced-head-ablations-2560games-80k/report.md`. This preserves the stage-specific assessment. Later sections supersede provisional recommendations where evidence changed.

### Matched architecture comparison

Same 2,560 training games (248,396 positions), 64 validation games (6,147 positions), seed 7980, batch 128, 16 trunk channels, 64 hidden features, ReLU, convolutional BatchNorm, dense dropout 0.1, AdamW betas (0.9, 0.99), epsilon 1e-8, weight decay 0.01, global clip 5, and 80,000 updates. Learning rate follows the first 80,000 steps of the previous 334,440-step schedule, including 5,820-step warmup from 1e-4 to 1e-3. No He initialization, dense BatchNorm, or normalization/bias decay exemption. The completed dropout-0.1 reference is copied from the prior run.

- Reference: two 3x3 convolutions, flatten, dense 64, ReLU, dropout, policy head.
- Residual: one 3x3 stem, three two-convolution post-activation residual blocks, same dense head. Seven spatial convolutions total, theoretical receptive field 15x15 versus 5x5 in the reference.
- Reduced head: original trunk, then 1x1 convolution 16 to 4 channels and ReLU before flattening, same dense hidden width and policy head.

All common initial stem/output weights are preserved; the residual variant also preserves the dense initialization and uses the original second convolution for its first residual convolution. Extra layers initialize under a forked CPU RNG, preserving the training RNG stream. This is a comparison at equal optimizer updates and data exposure, not equal compute.

#### Validation and interpretation limits

Actual batch hashes and every learning-rate value match the reference at every checkpoint. All gradients are finite and post-clip norms respect the threshold within float32 tolerance. All 39 repository tests passed, including identity shortcut gradients, architecture shapes, common initialization, and inference checkpoint reconstruction.

The legacy norm2 health field means the final residual branch BatchNorm for residual_3, but the second convolution BatchNorm for the other architectures. These have different roles, so their gamma values should not be treated as directly equivalent feature scales.

One seed, a heavily repeated training subset (about 41 passes), and 64 held-out games limit conclusions. The residual comparison changes depth and shortcut structure together; it does not isolate shortcuts from depth. No playing-strength evaluation is included.

#### Best residual checkpoint full legal probe

The best saved residual checkpoint (40,000 updates) has legal NLL 3.2629 and legal top-1 accuracy 22.53% on all 6,147 validation moves.

#### Assessment

The deeper residual architecture is the strongest accuracy candidate. It improved raw and legal move accuracy,
with only 3.5% more parameters, and its best saved validation loss was at 40,000 updates. Its final legal NLL
was worse than the reference despite higher accuracy; the 40,000-update checkpoint had better legal NLL
(3.2629) than the final residual checkpoint (3.3423).

It did not eliminate long-run drift. In updates 40,001–80,000, clipping rose to 12.84%, versus 0.06% in the
reference, and BatchNorm parameter gradient tails grew. Global gradient p95 was 6.02, maximum 14.94;
all gradients were finite. This is substantially milder than sustained 100% clipping, but it is not evidence
that the full-scale instability has been solved. Raw validation loss rose while training loss fell.

The reduced head is a parameter-saving tradeoff: 14.6% fewer parameters, slightly better raw NLL,
better legal NLL, stable gradients, but lower raw and legal top-1 accuracy. It does not justify replacing
the existing head solely to improve move accuracy.

Dense activation concentration remained similar across cases (top four features carry about 12–13% of
activity). However, the final residual trunk was more concentrated: four of sixteen channels carried 65.7%
of activity, versus 37.5% in the reference and 33.7% in the reduced-head model. No trunk channel was dormant
on the sampled observations. Residual dense dormant fraction was 7.8%, versus 3.1% and 0% respectively.
Thus increased accuracy should not be described as uniformly healthier internal statistics.

For the next architecture, favor the residual trunk with the existing dense head and dropout 0.1, using
validation-based checkpoint selection. The smaller-data run supports the architecture's accuracy benefit;
it does not determine the best LR schedule or stopping epoch for the full dataset.



<a id="stage-20"></a>

## 20. Residual late-training calibration and normalization diagnosis

Existing residual checkpoints were re-evaluated without new training or fitted temperatures. On the complete 6,147-position legal validation set, from 20k → 40k → 80k:

- Legal accuracy: **22.30% → 22.53% → 23.07%**.
- Mean top confidence: **34.40% → 35.14% → 37.10%**.
- Legal NLL: **3.2078 → 3.2629 → 3.3423**.
- Legal ECE (15 equal-width bins): **0.1210 → 0.1261 → 0.1403**.
- Brier score: **0.9000 → 0.9015 → 0.9041**.

The data support growing overconfidence/probability overfitting while top-1 accuracy improves. Best legal NLL, best raw NLL, and best accuracy occurred at different checkpoints (20k, 40k, 80k). It is incorrect to equate their objectives.

Fresh batch-stat evaluation did not rescue NLL: at 80k, eval with running statistics was **3.6239** versus **3.6839** with batch statistics, dropout disabled in both modes and running-buffer updates disabled. At 40k: **3.5724 versus 3.5887**. This weakens stale BN buffers as the simple primary explanation, but does not rule out all batch-stat effects. Dropout was after all BN layers, making the usual dropout-before-BN variance-shift mechanism a poor direct match.

Actual late relative updates decreased for stem, dense and policy parameters even as raw normalization-gradient tails grew; only the final branch BN relative update increased in that comparison. Raw gradient growth is not the same as runaway optimizer steps. The last residual branch’s gamma does not directly measure the entire feature scale because the shortcut remains. Literature suggested LR timing, calibration/label smoothing, and normalization controls as hypotheses; none was established as the cause.

<a id="stage-21"></a>

## 21. Faster residual LR decay

A matched residual follow-up changed cosine horizon **334,440 → 80,000** so decay actually reached 1e-5 within the observed run. Warmup remained 5,820 updates; all data, architecture, optimizer, seed and clipping settings stayed fixed. Full raw/legal validation ran every 5k (16 checks rather than four), preserving training RNG at added evaluations. Matching input hashes, warmup LR and identical 5k tensors were audited; additional RNG replay checks confirmed inserted evaluations did not alter dropout training state.

Earlier decay reduced late clipping **12.84% → 2.86%** and late max gradient **14.94 → 9.35**, but late mean gradient barely changed (**4.060 → 4.039**). Final raw/legal accuracy rose modestly, while final raw/legal NLL worsened and calibration did not improve. Best-checkpoint NLL differences were tiny and benefited from more selection opportunities; on the original shared checkpoints the old schedule had better best NLL. This directly contradicted the idea that earlier decay alone would solve probability deterioration.

The intervention also changed cumulative AdamW shrinkage: decay-only multipliers ~0.475 versus ~0.666, ignoring gradients. Therefore it did not isolate gradient step-size effects from regularization exposure. Some internal statistics improved without better NLL. The preserved detailed report contains all 16 checkpoints and the revised interpretation.

#### Residual CNN: faster learning-rate decay experiment

Results directory: `/Users/jesuscaraball0/code/school_code/67980/fow/out/experiments/residual-faster-cosine-decay-2560games-80k`. Same cached 2,560 training games (248,396 moves), 64 validation games (6,147 moves), seed 7980, batch 128, 16 channels / 64 hidden features, three residual blocks, default initialization, convolutional BN, dropout 0.1, AdamW (betas 0.9/0.99, eps 1e-8, weight decay 0.01), and global clip 5. Only the cosine horizon changes from 334,440 to 80,000 updates; warmup stays 5,820 steps (1e-4 to 1e-3), followed by decay to 1e-5.

Full raw and legal validation is evaluated every 5,000 updates. Additional evaluations preserve training RNG state; original 5k/20k/40k/80k evaluation points consume RNG as in the reference. All input hashes match at shared checkpoints, and the 5k checkpoint weights exactly reproduce the old run. No label smoothing or normalization changes.

![Residual decay comparison](/Users/jesuscaraball0/code/school_code/67980/fow/out/experiments/residual-faster-cosine-decay-2560games-80k/comparison.png)

##### Interpretation of the faster-decay result

**The faster decay reduced gradient tails but did not fix probability overfitting.** Over the identical
40,001–80,000-update window, clipping fell from 12.84% to 2.86%, and the maximum pre-clip norm fell from
14.94 to 9.35. Mean pre-clip gradient L2 was almost unchanged (4.060 versus 4.039), so this should not
be described as eliminating large gradients generally. Clipping still occurred on 5.0% of the final 5k updates.

Final raw accuracy increased by approximately 0.43 percentage points (22.22% to 22.65%), and final legal
accuracy by 0.44 points (23.07% to 23.51%). However, raw NLL worsened from 3.6239 to 3.6600 and legal NLL
from 3.3423 to 3.3815. Legal ECE was essentially unchanged (0.1403 versus 0.1424). The lower training LR
therefore did not deliver the hoped-for generalization/calibration improvement.

The best saved raw NLLs are nearly tied: 3.5724 at 40k in the reference versus 3.5687 at 25k with faster
decay. Best saved legal NLLs are also close: 3.2078 at 20k versus 3.1999 at 15k. The new run has sixteen
evaluations rather than four, so these tiny best-checkpoint differences are not evidence of superiority.
On the original four shared checkpoints, the previous schedule has better best raw and legal NLL.
The primary endpoint comparisons above use identical 80k budgets.

Several internal statistics improved without improving NLL. Final dense weight L2 was 39.50 versus
65.71, policy weight L2 837.19 versus 1226.11, and the last residual branch BN gamma median 0.298 versus
0.137. Top-four trunk activity share was 53.6% versus 65.7%; dense activity share remained about 11.9%
in both. Dense dormant fraction stayed 7.8%. Smaller norms and more distributed trunk activity should
not be equated with better probability predictions.

Actual late relative updates also decreased. Mean update/weight L2 for the stem fell from 0.0980% to
0.0286%, dense layer from 0.0964% to 0.0309%, policy from 0.00577% to 0.00176%, and last branch BN from
0.0743% to 0.0119%. These are means pooled across the same late window. All parameters and gradients
remained finite.

Changing LR also changes cumulative AdamW decay because each step multiplies updated parameters by
(1 - LR * weight_decay). Ignoring gradient updates, the accumulated multiplier is approximately 0.475
for the old schedule and 0.666 for the faster schedule. Thus the intervention changes both step sizes
and cumulative shrinkage; the results do not isolate these as separate causal mechanisms, and the BN
gamma difference must not be attributed solely to one of them.

**Revised conclusion:** sustained high LR was not sufficient to explain the validation-NLL deterioration.
The follow-up supports treating gradient-tail control and probability overfitting as distinct objectives.
Faster decay is a tradeoff: modestly higher move accuracy and fewer clipped updates, with no NLL or
calibration gain in this seed. Do not promote it as a universal fix or change production defaults on that claim.

For probability quality, retain legal-NLL-based checkpoint selection; the best legal-NLL checkpoint here is
15k, not the 80k accuracy checkpoint. The next targeted intervention would address confidence directly,
for example a controlled legal-action-aware label-smoothing test, or post-hoc temperature calibration on
separate calibration/evaluation games. Neither has been run in this follow-up. For residual optimization
questions, normalization-specific controls remain separate experiments rather than established remedies.

All 41 tests passed before launch. Actual batch hashes match the reference at all shared checkpoints;
warmup LR traces match exactly and the new final LR is 1e-5. The 5k model tensors reproduce exactly.
An independent RNG replay also verified at 10k and 15k that added evaluations consumed no training randomness.
The full validation calibration comparison and all sixteen checkpoint metrics are retained in JSON files.

<a id="stage-22"></a>

## 22. Revised interpretation and full-data residual launch decision

The user challenged an increasingly complicated set of proposed remedies. The simpler interpretation for the **small-data pilots** was ordinary repeated-data overfitting: ~248k correlated positions reused ~41 times, falling train NLL and rising validation NLL, with improving top-1 accuracy. Early checkpoint selection and more distinct games were sensible responses. However, that explanation was explicitly qualified: the prior full-data 8-epoch cluster run’s validation NLL kept improving, so its internal gradient growth was not established as the same overfitting problem.

The user chose to prioritize **accuracy**, retain the residual architecture, and use all data for up to 50 epochs. Production training then gained residual/dropout CLI arguments and `selection_metric`; the cluster residual script selected best_policy.pt by **legal top-1 on a fixed 8,192-position probe**, while raw validation metrics remained full-split. This is not selection by full-split legal accuracy. Historical production defaults remained loss-based unless explicitly overridden; historical experiment checkpoint names have their own meanings.

The selected run kept the tested 16/64 residual model, three blocks, convolutional BN, dropout .1, default initialization, AdamW (0.9,.99), eps1e-8, decay .01, batch128, global clip5, LR1e-4→1e-3→1e-5, warmup5,820 and cosine over all actual 50 epochs. Epoch-boundary resume including dropout RNG was tested against uninterrupted training. The 42-test suite passed at that point; script syntax and CUDA startup checks were provided. Local tests do not certify a remote cluster allocation, but the downloaded completion artifacts below establish that this run actually finished.

<a id="stage-23"></a>

## 23. Full-data residual: 50 epochs, job 27846286

The downloaded run **27846286** completed **50 epochs / 2,090,250 updates** in **9,325.9 seconds (~2.59 hours)** on the full split. It had 348,081 parameters. Best raw full-validation accuracy **27.806% at epoch 47**; best fixed-probe legal accuracy **28.772% at epoch 43** (best_policy.pt); best raw NLL **2.887580 at epoch 49**; final raw accuracy **27.79%**, NLL **2.8897**. These choices must not be conflated.

Validation NLL improved from **3.1168** to **2.8897**; train NLL finished **2.9825** with dropout active, so train-vs-val ordering is not a like-for-like deterministic loss comparison. This did not show the pilot’s classic late validation-loss overfitting pattern. More data improved held-out learning, but did not solve internal concentration.

Clipping was 100% from epoch 4 onward. Global gradient median grew **3.01 → 36.25**; largest observed norm **522.02** at epoch 15. Gradients remained finite. Final largest median layer norms included last branch BN2 **18.34**, stem BN **17.55**, second block BN2 **13.01**, dense **12.76**, first block BN2 **11.35**. Sampled relative optimizer updates decreased strongly as LR decayed.

On the final 512-observation diagnostic sample, the first ReLU had no dormant channels; the last residual block had **9/16 relatively dormant channels**, **91.57% zeros**, and **one channel carried 98.39% of mean absolute activity**. Dense features were far more balanced: 2/64 dormant, top-four share ~12.59%. Thus the clearest concentration moved to the late convolutional trunk; this is not “all layers collapsed.” A causal channel-ablation evaluation was proposed but **has not been run**.

Final stem BN gamma median ~0.0421; last branch BN gamma median ~0.00933, with one gamma ~1.955. Several interior running variances were small but finite. Dense/policy weight L2 ~386 / ~2,864. The counterfactual decay-only multiplier over this very long run was ~2.60e-5; this is not actual parameter shrinkage, since loss gradients continually update the weights. Scale imbalance is a plausible mechanism, not an established cause. Earlier no-decay tests were nearly neutral and fixed BN affine was worse, so blaming normalization weight decay as settled would overstate the evidence.

This full-data run corrects the earlier overly broad “we mainly need more data” interpretation. Distinct data helped generalization but did not cure the trunk concentration or sustained normalization-gradient burden.

### Full-data residual run 27846286

Completed 50 epochs in 2.59 hours, 2,090,250 optimizer updates. Model: 348,081
parameters, 16 channels, hidden size 64, three residual blocks, convolutional
BatchNorm, dropout 0.1, default initialization. All 55,250 training games
(5,350,942 positions); 6,141 validation games (595,179 positions).

| Metric | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Best full-validation raw accuracy | 27.81%, epoch 47 |
| Best fixed-probe legal accuracy | 28.77%, epoch 43; saved best_policy.pt |
| Best full-validation raw NLL | 2.8876, epoch 49 |
| Final raw accuracy / NLL | 27.79% / 2.8897 |
| Final training NLL | 2.9825, measured with dropout active |
| Final legal-probe accuracy / NLL | 28.54% / 2.7003 |
| Clipped updates | 100% from epoch 4 onward |
| Pre-clip global gradient median | 3.01 at epoch 1; 36.25 at epoch 50 |
| Largest gradient observed | 522.02, epoch 15 |
| Final last-trunk activation zeros | 91.57% |
| Final last-trunk dormant channels | 9/16, relative activity threshold on 512 observations |
| Single-channel share of last-trunk mean absolute activity | 98.39% |
| Final dense ReLU dormant features | 2/64 |
| Final dense top-four activity share | 12.59% |

Validation loss improved from 3.1168 to 2.8897, with its best at epoch 49.
This is not the pilot's late validation-loss overfitting pattern. Training loss
is measured with dropout active, whereas validation is evaluated with dropout
inactive; their ordering does not establish leakage or lack of learning.

The internal problem persists at full data scale. First-layer ReLU has no
dormant channels; dense features remain relatively balanced. Concentration is
strongest near the end of the convolutional residual trunk. Activity share is
not causal contribution: a channel-ablation evaluation is needed to establish
how much predictions depend on that channel.

Largest final median layer gradients are last-block norm2 (18.34), stem norm
(17.55), second-block norm2 (13.01), dense layer (12.76), first-block norm2
(11.35). BatchNorm affine parameters are prominent. Stem gamma median is
0.0421 and last-block norm2 gamma median 0.00933, while one last-block gamma
is 1.955. Dense and policy weight L2 norms are approximately 386 and 2,864.
Running variances are small in several interior blocks, but finite; these
alone do not establish broken statistics. All recorded gradients are finite.
Actual relative updates shrink with LR; dense median relative update drops
from 0.001738 in epoch 1 to 0.000001336 in epoch 50. High raw gradients do not
mean all parameters receive runaway updates. Global clipping rescales every
layer's raw gradient; Adam's adaptive moments mean that this rescaling cannot
be read as a proportional reduction in actual parameter updates.

A plausible mechanism is scale imbalance among normalized trunk features and
the dense classifier. This is a hypothesis, not a causal diagnosis. Literature
shows normalization and regularization interact through parameter scale and
effective learning rate, but does not prove the cause in this AdamW run:
https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.05350
https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.05101

Long-run decay exposure differs substantially from the short pilots: the
counterfactual decay-only multiplier over this run is about 2.60e-5. This
ignores all loss gradients and is not an estimate of actual parameter shrinkage.
It motivates controlling duration when testing regularization, rather than
assuming unchanged weight_decay means an identical effect across budgets.

The earlier plain 64/256 CNN achieved raw accuracy 30.98% and NLL 2.5810 in
8 epochs. This residual run does not beat it on these metrics, despite more
updates. It has approximately 6.2 times fewer parameters, different architecture,
dropout and schedule, so this is not a controlled residual-vs-plain comparison.
The best legal accuracy comes from a fixed 8,192-position probe, not all held-out
positions; epoch 43 is not proven best on the full legal validation set.

Next: evaluate the saved best models on matched held-out games and measure
sensitivity to ablating the dominant trunk channel. If testing a training fix,
run a matched residual baseline versus excluding normalization affine and
bias parameters from decay, long enough to reproduce the epoch-2/3 onset.
The earlier short pilot found little benefit from that exemption, so it is a
hypothesis test, not an established solution. Do not increase clipping threshold
or launch another 50-epoch run solely on the basis of the current diagnostics.
More data improved held-out learning but did not remove feature concentration.

## 24. Best residual versus best full CNN: 100 games

The existing evaluator played the saved best full-data residual (epoch43, selected by legal probe accuracy) against the saved best clip5/BN full CNN (epoch8, selected by raw loss, also that run’s best raw accuracy). Both used the same shared runtime, legal/visible-safety move filtering, sampling temperature .9, alternating colors, 180+2 clocks, and default initial positions. Separate frozen bundles preserved the original weights. This tests these checkpoints, not every model called “full CNN” or “residual.”

#### Head-to-head: residual versus best full CNN

Played 100 games using evaluate.py, alternating colors (50 each), 180+2 clocks,
max 1000 plies, sampling temperature 0.9, shared current observation-based move
filtering. Residual: best_policy.pt from run 27846286, epoch 43, selected by
legal accuracy on 8192 fixed held-out positions. Full CNN: best_policy.pt from
27800942, epoch 8, selected by raw validation loss (also best raw accuracy).
Original checkpoints were preserved; evaluation used separate frozen bundles.

Residual: 32 wins, 68 losses, zero draws. As white: 14/50 wins; as black:
18/50 wins. No bot failures. All games terminated with King capturable, the
fog-of-war referee's terminal condition. Mean length 63.6 plies (12–139).
Elapsed 878.2 seconds. Approximate 95% Wilson interval for the residual win
probability in this matchup: 23.7%–41.7%, assuming independent games.
This is one stochastic matchup with default starting boards, not a broad
strength rating or a causal test of the training issues.

The full CNN wins clearly in this series. The residual's 348081 parameters
are substantially fewer than the plain CNN's 2146817; architecture, dropout,
training duration and checkpoint criterion also differ. Thus this comparison
does not establish residual architecture as worse, or capacity as the only
cause of the gap.

A useful next capacity test is channels=64, hidden_size=256, residual_blocks=3,
dropout=0.1: 2332353 parameters, close to the plain CNN's capacity. Keep the
remaining recipe fixed for that experiment and inspect early checkpoints
before committing to another long run. A larger residual is a capacity test,
not an established cure for the normalization gradient / feature concentration
problem. It may reproduce those problems. No larger training run was launched.

The result, **32 residual wins / 68 full-CNN wins / zero draws**, was consistent across both colors (14/50 white wins, 18/50 black wins). No bot failures; all games ended King capturable. The residual win probability’s approximate Wilson 95% interval was **23.7%–41.7%** under an independent-game assumption. It is one matchup, not an Elo rating or evidence that all residual architectures are weaker. The full CNN had 2,147,073 parameters including BN affine weights (~6.2 times as many as the residual; 2,146,817 is the no-BN plain count), different dropout, duration and schedule. No causal isolation of model capacity was performed.

## 26. Current evidence, open questions, and superseded claims

### Findings supported by the experiments

1. The feedforward policy can outperform the recurrent policy; recurrence alone did not establish better imitation loss or playing strength. Small-data reset-memory probes showed both harmful and useful history depending on data regime.
2. Argmax sampling from identical starts produced deterministic draw cycles; stochastic legal-action sampling removed that particular failure pattern. Temperature .9 was a choice, not an optimized result.
3. Visible king safety and complete hidden-board safety are different. King-capturable terminations alone do not establish an implementation failure.
4. More distinct training data plus more training improved the early small model substantially; the experimental design did not isolate those contributions.
5. Larger models learned faster under some fixed-update budgets; they also showed earlier small-data NLL overfitting. Medium size was a practical compromise, not a proven universal optimum.
6. AdamW at unchanged high LR slightly improved the first size sweep’s losses. Lower LR1e-4 was worse at the short fixed budget. Neither result establishes one optimizer/LR as universally best.
7. He-normal convolution initialization did not help the matched medium run.
8. Convolutional BN improved the short larger-data run; later full-data training revealed sustained affine-gradient growth and concentration. A short successful pilot did not certify long-run stability.
9. Dense BN and dropout redistributed dense activity. Better concentration metrics did not consistently mean better NLL or accuracy. Dropout .1 was the best balanced dropout candidate in the controlled subset runs.
10. Fixing BN affine parameters hurt; excluding norm/bias decay was nearly neutral in the tested plain-model stress regime. Neither supports a settled “BN weight decay is the root cause” claim.
11. Residual depth improved subset raw/legal accuracy at nearly unchanged parameter count; it did not eliminate normalization-gradient tails or trunk concentration. Depth and shortcuts were changed together.
12. Reduced head saved parameters and improved legal NLL at an accuracy cost.
13. Earlier cosine decay reduced gradient tails and clipping without improving final NLL/calibration. Tiny best-checkpoint differences were confounded by denser validation selection.
14. The full-data 16/64 residual kept improving validation loss but developed severe late-trunk concentration and clipping. Small-data overfitting and full-data scale imbalance cannot be treated as one demonstrated mechanism.
15. The best clip5/BN full CNN beat the small residual 68–32 in the recorded matchup. Capacity, schedule, dropout and checkpoint selection differ; this does not isolate architectural superiority.
16. No observation establishes that near-normal weight histograms, positive activations, zero clipping, or any fixed parameter/data ratio is the right training objective.

### Corrections to earlier conversational interpretations

- “Both losses went down” in the first AdamW comparison was correct; the improvement was small, not absent.
- The first full cluster CNN was actually eight epochs, despite earlier discussion of a bigger run. The later residual was actually 50.
- We did not originally have common dropout and clip5 on both models. Historical feedforward clipping was a no-op; recurrent clipping was1; later production explicitly used5.
- Sparse ReLU histograms alone did not prove all features dead. Later channel activity/concentration measurements provide more precise evidence.
- The 80k/334k stress schedule was intentionally truncated, not broken; earlier decay was tested and did not solve probability overfitting.
- The pilot’s late validation-NLL overfitting did not explain the continuously improving full-data curves. More data was a reasonable test, not a complete diagnosis.
- The full CNN was not established as “too big” on the full dataset. It generalized better than the smaller residual and won the matchup, despite concerning internals.
- The suggested 64/256 residual was a capacity-matched comparison, not a recommendation derived from an optimal scaling law. The user chose32/128 as a more conservative next test.
- Historical `best_policy.pt` is not one universal criterion: old runs used raw NLL, the production residual launch explicitly uses fixed-probe legal accuracy, and the decay experiment saves multiple separately named optima.

### Unresolved questions and unrun proposals

The following remain hypotheses/proposals: whether the dominant late residual channel is causally necessary; whether normalization scale drift causes the concentration or follows it; whether a longer residual-specific norm/bias decay exemption helps; lower BN affine LR; GroupNorm; legal-action-aware label smoothing; post-hoc temperature calibration on separate calibration/test games; zero-gamma residual initialization; alternative spatial policy heads; more seeds; a genuinely untouched test split; broader opponents/openings; PPO training. These must not be described as completed results.

No need to optimize solely for a low clipping fraction: clipping all raw gradients at a step does not directly bound AdamW’s parameter update because its adaptive moments matter. Judge validation accuracy, legal NLL/calibration, actual updates, activation concentration and playing strength separately. Existing evidence supports retaining learned BN affine parameters and default convolution initialization while testing the medium residual’s capacity; it does not establish that widening will fix the internal issue.

### Literature consulted and limits of applicability

- [Guo et al. (2017), On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v70/guo17a.html). Supports separating improving accuracy from worsening NLL/calibration; temperature scaling is post-hoc, not a fix for training gradients.

- [van Laarhoven (2017), L2 Regularization versus Batch and Weight Normalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.05350). Normalization changes how parameter scale, regularization and effective LR interact. Does not establish that BN affine decay causes this AdamW failure mode.

- [Lobacheva et al. (2021), On the Periodic Behavior of Neural Network Training with Batch Normalization and Weight Decay](https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2021/hash/b433da1b32b5ca96c0ba7fcb9edba97d-Abstract.html). A possible scale/effective-LR mechanism; SGD-focused periodic behavior is not directly demonstrated in these AdamW trajectories.

- [He et al. (2016), Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385). Motivates residual depth; our controlled ablation combines greater depth and shortcuts, so their individual effects are not isolated.

- [He et al. (2019), Bag of Tricks for Image Classification with Convolutional Neural Networks](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content_CVPR_2019/papers/He_Bag_of_Tricks_for_Image_Classification_with_Convolutional_Neural_Networks_CVPR_2019_paper.pdf). Practical CNN recipes/initialization/schedules motivate tests; published settings are not demonstrated optima for this game task.

- [Ioffe and Szegedy (2015), Batch Normalization](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v37/ioffe15.html). BN is used for convolutional and dense layers; common practice is not evidence that dense BN will improve our predictions.

- [Srivastava et al. (2014), Dropout](https://jmlr.org/papers/v15/srivastava14a.html). Motivates reducing feature coadaptation. Our measured effects depend on probability and placement.

- [Li et al. (2019), Understanding the Disharmony Between Dropout and Batch Normalization by Variance Shift](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.05134). Mechanism is most relevant when dropout feeds BN; our hidden dropout follows BN.

- [Wu and He (2018), Group Normalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.08494). Batch-independent normalization is an unrun alternative, not an established fix.

- [Müller et al. (2019), When Does Label Smoothing Help?](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.02629). Motivates an unrun confidence intervention. Uniform target smoothing over4096 moves would assign mass to illegal actions; a legal-aware formulation would need testing.

- [Loshchilov and Hutter (2019), Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.05101). AdamW separates gradient adaptation and parameter decay; fixed decay coefficient does not imply equal cumulative exposure across schedules/durations.

- [Loshchilov and Hutter (2017), SGDR](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.03983). Cosine scheduling reference; our no-restart schedule is a chosen recipe, not a directly transferred optimal result.

- [Hestness et al. (2017), Deep Learning Scaling is Predictable, Empirically](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.00409). Supports measuring task-specific scaling, not prescribing a universal moves-per-parameter ratio.

- [Hoffmann et al. (2022), Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556). Language-model token/parameter scaling should not be used as a numerical optimum for correlated chess-observation CNN examples.

- [Leela Chess Zero historical CNN architecture documentation](https://draft.lczero.org/dev/old/nn/). Historical game-network design context, not evidence that every current system uses the same architecture or our exact settings.

### Reproducibility and limits

Seeds, model sizes, data paths, batch sizes, optimizers, schedules, probe counts, and artifact paths are recorded in each run. The controlled suites verified actual input hashes/LR traces; the residual faster-decay run additionally verified evaluation RNG preservation. These are mostly **one-training-seed** experiments, not statistical estimates over initializations. Runs with different subsets, schedules, training durations, clipping implementations, architectures, or probe sizes should not be directly ranked as if all factors were controlled. The generic stress-test runner saves optimizer/scheduler states but does not save the complete BatchStream cursor/generator needed to promise exact midstream resume; production epoch-boundary resume has a separate tested implementation.

No new training, games, or architecture changes were performed while consolidating this document. The medium residual cluster run is pending.

#### Full-data residual run 27846286

Completed 50 epochs in 2.59 hours, 2,090,250 optimizer updates. Model: 348,081
parameters, 16 channels, hidden size 64, three residual blocks, convolutional
BatchNorm, dropout 0.1, default initialization. All 55,250 training games
(5,350,942 positions); 6,141 validation games (595,179 positions).

| Metric | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Best full-validation raw accuracy | 27.81%, epoch 47 |
| Best fixed-probe legal accuracy | 28.77%, epoch 43; saved best_policy.pt |
| Best full-validation raw NLL | 2.8876, epoch 49 |
| Final raw accuracy / NLL | 27.79% / 2.8897 |
| Final training NLL | 2.9825, measured with dropout active |
| Final legal-probe accuracy / NLL | 28.54% / 2.7003 |
| Clipped updates | 100% from epoch 4 onward |
| Pre-clip global gradient median | 3.01 at epoch 1; 36.25 at epoch 50 |
| Largest gradient observed | 522.02, epoch 15 |
| Final last-trunk activation zeros | 91.57% |
| Final last-trunk dormant channels | 9/16, relative activity threshold on 512 observations |
| Single-channel share of last-trunk mean absolute activity | 98.39% |
| Final dense ReLU dormant features | 2/64 |
| Final dense top-four activity share | 12.59% |

Validation loss improved from 3.1168 to 2.8897, with its best at epoch 49.
This is not the pilot's late validation-loss overfitting pattern. Training loss
is measured with dropout active, whereas validation is evaluated with dropout
inactive; their ordering does not establish leakage or lack of learning.

The internal problem persists at full data scale. First-layer ReLU has no
dormant channels; dense features remain relatively balanced. Concentration is
strongest near the end of the convolutional residual trunk. Activity share is
not causal contribution: a channel-ablation evaluation is needed to establish
how much predictions depend on that channel.

Largest final median layer gradients are last-block norm2 (18.34), stem norm
(17.55), second-block norm2 (13.01), dense layer (12.76), first-block norm2
(11.35). BatchNorm affine parameters are prominent. Stem gamma median is
0.0421 and last-block norm2 gamma median 0.00933, while one last-block gamma
is 1.955. Dense and policy weight L2 norms are approximately 386 and 2,864.
Running variances are small in several interior blocks, but finite; these
alone do not establish broken statistics. All recorded gradients are finite.
Actual relative updates shrink with LR; dense median relative update drops
from 0.001738 in epoch 1 to 0.000001336 in epoch 50. High raw gradients do not
mean all parameters receive runaway updates. Global clipping rescales every
layer's raw gradient; Adam's adaptive moments mean that this rescaling cannot
be read as a proportional reduction in actual parameter updates.

A plausible mechanism is scale imbalance among normalized trunk features and
the dense classifier. This is a hypothesis, not a causal diagnosis. Literature
shows normalization and regularization interact through parameter scale and
effective learning rate, but does not prove the cause in this AdamW run:
https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.05350
https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.05101

Long-run decay exposure differs substantially from the short pilots: the
counterfactual decay-only multiplier over this run is about 2.60e-5. This
ignores all loss gradients and is not an estimate of actual parameter shrinkage.
It motivates controlling duration when testing regularization, rather than
assuming unchanged weight_decay means an identical effect across budgets.

The earlier plain 64/256 CNN achieved raw accuracy 30.98% and NLL 2.5810 in
8 epochs. This residual run does not beat it on these metrics, despite more
updates. It has approximately 6.2 times fewer parameters, different architecture,
dropout and schedule, so this is not a controlled residual-vs-plain comparison.
The best legal accuracy comes from a fixed 8,192-position probe, not all held-out
positions; epoch 43 is not proven best on the full legal validation set.

Next: evaluate the saved best models on matched held-out games and measure
sensitivity to ablating the dominant trunk channel. If testing a training fix,
run a matched residual baseline versus excluding normalization affine and
bias parameters from decay, long enough to reproduce the epoch-2/3 onset.
The earlier short pilot found little benefit from that exemption, so it is a
hypothesis test, not an established solution. Do not increase clipping threshold
or launch another 50-epoch run solely on the basis of the current diagnostics.
More data improved held-out learning but did not remove feature concentration.

does not establish residual architecture as worse, or capacity as the only
cause of the gap.

A useful next capacity test is channels=64, hidden_size=256, residual_blocks=3,
dropout=0.1: 2332353 parameters, close to the plain CNN's capacity. Keep the
remaining recipe fixed for that experiment and inspect early checkpoints
before committing to another long run. A larger residual is a capacity test,
not an established cure for the normalization gradient / feature concentration
problem. It may reproduce those problems. No larger training run was launched.

##### Residual CNN: faster learning-rate decay experiment

Results directory: `/Users/jesuscaraball0/code/school_code/67980/fow/out/experiments/residual-faster-cosine-decay-2560games-80k`. Same cached 2,560 training games (248,396 moves), 64 validation games (6,147 moves), seed 7980, batch 128, 16 channels / 64 hidden features, three residual blocks, default initialization, convolutional BN, dropout 0.1, AdamW (betas 0.9/0.99, eps 1e-8, weight decay 0.01), and global clip 5. Only the cosine horizon changes from 334,440 to 80,000 updates; warmup stays 5,820 steps (1e-4 to 1e-3), followed by decay to 1e-5.

Full raw and legal validation is evaluated every 5,000 updates. Additional evaluations preserve training RNG state; original 5k/20k/40k/80k evaluation points consume RNG as in the reference. All input hashes match at shared checkpoints, and the 5k checkpoint weights exactly reproduce the old run. No label smoothing or normalization changes.

| Schedule | Best saved raw NLL | Update | Final raw NLL | Final raw accuracy | Final legal NLL | Final legal accuracy |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|

| Faster decay | 3.5687 | 25,000 | 3.6600 | 22.65% | 3.3815 | 23.51% |

The new run has denser checkpoint selection. For a like-for-like check among the original four checkpoints, its best raw NLL is 3.6002; best legal NLL is 3.2789 versus 3.2078 in the reference.

Best raw NLL remains `best_policy.pt`. Best legal NLL is `best_legal_nll_policy.pt` at 15,000 updates (3.1999); best legal accuracy is `best_accuracy_policy.pt` at 80,000 updates (23.51%). Best raw accuracy is saved separately as `best_raw_accuracy_policy.pt`.

Calibration uses T=1 and the complete legal action masks on the same validation games (15 equal-width ECE bins, no fitted temperature). One seed and 64 validation games limit generalization claims. No arena evaluation or production-default changes.

![Residual decay comparison](/Users/jesuscaraball0/code/school_code/67980/fow/out/experiments/residual-faster-cosine-decay-2560games-80k/comparison.png)

###### Interpretation of the faster-decay result

**The faster decay reduced gradient tails but did not fix probability overfitting.** Over the identical
40,001–80,000-update window, clipping fell from 12.84% to 2.86%, and the maximum pre-clip norm fell from
14.94 to 9.35. Mean pre-clip gradient L2 was almost unchanged (4.060 versus 4.039), so this should not
be described as eliminating large gradients generally. Clipping still occurred on 5.0% of the final 5k updates.

Final raw accuracy increased by approximately 0.43 percentage points (22.22% to 22.65%), and final legal
accuracy by 0.44 points (23.07% to 23.51%). However, raw NLL worsened from 3.6239 to 3.6600 and legal NLL
from 3.3423 to 3.3815. Legal ECE was essentially unchanged (0.1403 versus 0.1424). The lower training LR
therefore did not deliver the hoped-for generalization/calibration improvement.

The best saved raw NLLs are nearly tied: 3.5724 at 40k in the reference versus 3.5687 at 25k with faster
decay. Best saved legal NLLs are also close: 3.2078 at 20k versus 3.1999 at 15k. The new run has sixteen
evaluations rather than four, so these tiny best-checkpoint differences are not evidence of superiority.
On the original four shared checkpoints, the previous schedule has better best raw and legal NLL.
The primary endpoint comparisons above use identical 80k budgets.

Several internal statistics improved without improving NLL. Final dense weight L2 was 39.50 versus
65.71, policy weight L2 837.19 versus 1226.11, and the last residual branch BN gamma median 0.298 versus
0.137. Top-four trunk activity share was 53.6% versus 65.7%; dense activity share remained about 11.9%
in both. Dense dormant fraction stayed 7.8%. Smaller norms and more distributed trunk activity should
not be equated with better probability predictions.

Actual late relative updates also decreased. Mean update/weight L2 for the stem fell from 0.0980% to
0.0286%, dense layer from 0.0964% to 0.0309%, policy from 0.00577% to 0.00176%, and last branch BN from
0.0743% to 0.0119%. These are means pooled across the same late window. All parameters and gradients
remained finite.

Changing LR also changes cumulative AdamW decay because each step multiplies updated parameters by
(1 - LR * weight_decay). Ignoring gradient updates, the accumulated multiplier is approximately 0.475
for the old schedule and 0.666 for the faster schedule. Thus the intervention changes both step sizes
and cumulative shrinkage; the results do not isolate these as separate causal mechanisms, and the BN
gamma difference must not be attributed solely to one of them.

**Revised conclusion:** sustained high LR was not sufficient to explain the validation-NLL deterioration.
The follow-up supports treating gradient-tail control and probability overfitting as distinct objectives.
Faster decay is a tradeoff: modestly higher move accuracy and fewer clipped updates, with no NLL or
calibration gain in this seed. Do not promote it as a universal fix or change production defaults on that claim.

For probability quality, retain legal-NLL-based checkpoint selection; the best legal-NLL checkpoint here is
15k, not the 80k accuracy checkpoint. The next targeted intervention would address confidence directly,
for example a controlled legal-action-aware label-smoothing test, or post-hoc temperature calibration on
separate calibration/evaluation games. Neither has been run in this follow-up. For residual optimization
questions, normalization-specific controls remain separate experiments rather than established remedies.

All 41 tests passed before launch. Actual batch hashes match the reference at all shared checkpoints;
warmup LR traces match exactly and the new final LR is 1e-5. The 5k model tensors reproduce exactly.
An independent RNG replay also verified at 10k and 15k that added evaluations consumed no training randomness.
The full validation calibration comparison and all sixteen checkpoint metrics are retained in JSON files.

Source content SHA256: `52d5068e48bf1f04c57537e7b475e6558046022b517625a6265dd1ca08b86ad2`.

#### Stability ablation results

Four matched runs: 16 channels / 64 features, 2,560 training games, 64 validation games (6,147 moves), seed 7980, batch 128, AdamW (0.9, 0.99), epsilon 1e-8, weight decay 0.01, and global clipping at 5.

Each ran 80,000 updates from the beginning of the cluster run's 334,440-update LR schedule. Inputs and order match across all cases. The smaller training dataset is repeated about 41 times.

| Case | Best observed val loss | Best update | Final val loss | Final accuracy | Final legal NLL | Late clipping | Top-four dense activity |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Baseline | 3.7138 | 40,000 | 3.7915 | 20.7% | 3.5297 | 0.0% | 47.6% |
| No decay on norms/bias | 3.7140 | 40,000 | 3.7809 | 20.6% | 3.5089 | 0.0% | 47.6% |
| Fixed BN affine | 3.8039 | 20,000 | 4.0995 | 18.9% | 3.7737 | 42.8% | 49.3% |
| Dense BatchNorm | 3.6913 | 20,000 | 3.8004 | 20.3% | 3.5143 | 0.0% | 11.9% |

Late clipping covers updates 40,001–80,000. Activation metrics use a fixed random sample of 512 held-out moves; final legal metrics cover all 6,147 validation moves.

Dense normalization reduces activity concentration from 47.6% to 11.9% and late median gradient norm from 3.41 to 2.82. Its best validation loss improves slightly, but final validation loss and accuracy do not improve. Excluding normalization/bias from decay is almost neutral. Fixing BN affine parameters worsens validation and increases late clipping.

Limitation: the smaller baseline does not reproduce the full run's near-universal clipping. These results support dense normalization as a feature-balance intervention but do not establish a fix for the full-model instability. One seed, substantial small-data overfitting, and best values selected from saved checkpoints.

Next: retain learned BN affine parameters. Confirm dense normalization against the full architecture and intended LR horizon through 80k–120k updates, tracking clipping, per-layer gradient shares, BN gamma/beta, and feature concentration. The weight-decay change is not a proven fix.

Reproduce: `.venv/bin/python training/stability_experiment.py`
